questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How adults can learn to speak Welsh quickly
Indigenous languages and one woman's effort to save hers
Why English is the most important language in the world
How young children learn to read and write at school
questions.why: They discuss indigenous languages disappearing and Mshkogaabwid Kwe's effort to keep hers alive.

questions.q: Why does Neil mention the road sign in Wales?
options: As an example of an indigenous language that has survived
To complain that the Welsh road signs are too hard to read
To show that nobody in Wales speaks Welsh any more
To explain how he got lost driving on his trip to Wales
questions.why: Neil says Welsh is a good example of an indigenous language that has survived.

questions.q: What does Sam say happens when an indigenous language disappears?
options: People quickly learn another local language
Nothing important is lost
The culture linked to it disappears too
It is usually replaced by Welsh
questions.why: Sam says when an indigenous language disappears, 'so too does the culture'.

questions.q: When did Mshkogaabwid Kwe learn Anishinaabemowin?
options: As a young child at home
At school in Canada
From her four-year-old daughter
Later in life, as an adult
questions.why: She grew up speaking English and only learned Anishinaabemowin later, as an adult.

questions.q: What made Mshkogaabwid feel great joy after a couple of months of learning?
options: Reading a whole book in the language
Understanding a complete prayer at a ceremony
Teaching a class of children
Speaking to her ancestors' friends
questions.why: She says she was able to understand one full prayer at a ceremony feast, which gave her glee.

questions.q: What problem did Mshkogaabwid notice with her daughter?
options: She refused to speak to anyone at all
She forgot all her English at day care
She didn't like going to day care
She began using much more English
questions.why: She says day care influenced her English, so her daughter was speaking a lot of English.

questions.q: What rule does Mshkogaabwid's family have at home?
options: They speak only Anishinaabemowin
They speak English and Anishinaabemowin equally
They only speak English at dinner
They don't watch English TV
questions.why: She describes an 'immersion home' where they only speak Anishinaabemowin in the home.

questions.q: According to Sam, what does Mshkogaabwid believe speaking the language gives her children?
options: Better marks at school and more job choices
More chances to travel and meet other people
A sense of family history and their culture
A way to avoid having to learn English
questions.why: Sam says she believes it gives them a sense of family history and preserves her culture.
